questions.stem: What does a wave transfer from one place to another?
options: Particles of the medium, at the wave speed
Energy, without a net transfer of matter
Matter, without any transfer of energy
Both energy and matter, in equal amounts
questions.explanation: A wave carries energy from the source while the particles of the medium only vibrate about their rest positions. A cork on a pond bobs up and down as ripples pass but is not carried along with them.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a mechanical wave?
options: An oscillation of electric and magnetic fields that needs no medium at all
A disturbance that travels through a medium by the vibration of its particles
A disturbance that can travel through a vacuum as easily as through matter
A stream of particles carried all the way from the source to the receiver
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves, such as sound and waves on a string, need a medium because they pass energy from particle to particle. They cannot travel through a vacuum, unlike electromagnetic waves.

questions.stem: How do the particles of a medium move in a transverse wave?
options: In circles centred on the source of the wave
At right angles to the direction the energy travels
Parallel to the direction the energy travels
In the direction of travel, at the speed of the wave
questions.explanation: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, forming crests and troughs. In a longitudinal wave they vibrate parallel to it, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.stem: An earthquake sends out seismic P waves and S waves. How are these classified?
options: P waves are longitudinal and S waves are transverse
P waves are transverse and S waves are longitudinal
Both P waves and S waves are longitudinal waves
Both P waves and S waves are transverse waves
questions.explanation: P (primary) waves are compression waves, with rock vibrating along the direction of travel, so they are longitudinal. S (secondary) waves shake the rock at right angles to their direction of travel, so they are transverse.

questions.stem: A plucked guitar string makes a sound that travels to a listener. How are the two waves classified?
options: The wave on the string is longitudinal; the sound in the air is transverse
Both are transverse, because the sound copies the motion of the string
Both are longitudinal, because all sound waves begin as compressions
The wave on the string is transverse; the sound in the air is longitudinal
questions.explanation: The string moves sideways while the wave travels along it, so that wave is transverse. The vibrating string pushes on the air, sending out compressions and rarefactions in the direction of travel, so sound in air is longitudinal.

questions.stem: In a sound wave, what is a compression?
options: The highest point reached by particles above their rest position
The distance between two neighbouring regions of low pressure
A region where the particles are closer together than normal
A region where the particles are further apart than normal
questions.explanation: A compression is a region of higher pressure, where the particles are crowded together. A rarefaction is the opposite, where they are spread out. Crests are features of transverse waves, not longitudinal ones.

questions.stem: In a sound wave in air, neighbouring compressions are 0.50 m apart. What is the frequency of the sound? Use v = 346 m s⁻¹.
options: 692 Hz
173 Hz
questions.explanation: The distance between neighbouring compressions is one wavelength, so f = v/λ = 346/0.50 = 692 Hz. Treating 0.50 m as half a wavelength gives 1384 Hz, and multiplying v by λ gives 173.

questions.stem: A displacement-distance graph of a transverse wave shows 6.0 cm between the top of a crest and the bottom of a trough, and 0.80 m between neighbouring crests. What are the amplitude and wavelength?
options: Amplitude 3.0 cm, wavelength 0.80 m
Amplitude 6.0 cm, wavelength 0.80 m
Amplitude 3.0 cm, wavelength 1.6 m
Amplitude 6.0 cm, wavelength 0.40 m
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position, half of the crest-to-trough distance: 3.0 cm. Wavelength is the distance between neighbouring crests, 0.80 m. Taking the full crest-to-trough height as the amplitude is a common slip.

questions.stem: A displacement-time graph for one particle in a wave shows exactly 5 complete oscillations in 0.020 s. What is the frequency of the wave?
options: 50 Hz
250 Hz
questions.explanation: The period is 0.020/5 = 0.0040 s, so f = 1/T = 1/0.0040 = 250 Hz. The value 0.0040 is the period in seconds, not the frequency, and 50 Hz uses the whole 0.020 s as one period.

questions.stem: For the same wave, a displacement-distance graph repeats every 2.0 m and a displacement-time graph for one particle repeats every 0.50 s. What is the wave speed?
options: 1.0 m s⁻¹
2.5 m s⁻¹
4.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The displacement-distance graph gives the wavelength, 2.0 m, and the displacement-time graph gives the period, 0.50 s. So v = λ/T = 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 m s⁻¹. Multiplying the two gives 1.0, which mixes up period and frequency.

questions.stem: What is the period of a wave with a frequency of 200 Hz?
questions.explanation: Period and frequency are reciprocals: T = 1/f = 1/200 = 0.0050 s. A wave with a high frequency has a short period.

questions.stem: Ocean swell travels at 12 m s⁻¹ with a wavelength of 60 m. What is the period of the waves?
questions.explanation: The frequency is f = v/λ = 12/60 = 0.20 Hz, so the period is T = 1/f = 5.0 s. The value 0.20 is the frequency in hertz, not the period, and 720 comes from multiplying v by λ.

questions.stem: A student doubles the frequency of waves on a long spring without changing the spring or its tension. What happens?
options: The speed stays the same and the wavelength doubles
The speed stays the same and the wavelength halves
The speed doubles and the wavelength stays the same
The speed halves and the wavelength stays the same
questions.explanation: Wave speed depends on the medium, which has not changed. Since v = fλ, doubling f at constant v halves λ. The source sets the frequency, but it does not set the speed.

questions.stem: Neighbouring compressions on a stretched slinky are 0.30 m apart, and four compressions pass a point each second. What is the speed of the wave?
options: 13 m s⁻¹
1.2 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The wavelength is 0.30 m and the frequency is 4 Hz, so v = fλ = 4 × 0.30 = 1.2 m s⁻¹. Dividing the wavelength by the frequency gives 0.075, and 13 comes from dividing the frequency by the wavelength.

questions.stem: Water waves pass from deep water into shallow water, where they travel more slowly. What happens to them?
options: Their speed and wavelength decrease, and their frequency decreases too
Their speed and wavelength decrease, and their frequency stays the same
Their speed and frequency decrease, and their wavelength stays the same
Their speed decreases, and their frequency and wavelength both increase
questions.explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary. With v = fλ, a lower speed at the same frequency means a shorter wavelength. If the waves meet the boundary at an angle, they also change direction, which is refraction.

questions.stem: A pulse travels along a rope and reflects from an end tied firmly to a wall. How does the reflected pulse compare with the incoming pulse?
options: It is inverted and travels back at a slower speed
It is upright and travels back at a faster speed
It is inverted and travels back at the same speed
It is upright and travels back at the same speed
questions.explanation: At a fixed end the rope cannot move, so the wall exerts an opposite force and the pulse returns upside down. The medium is unchanged, so the speed is unchanged. A pulse reflected from a free end returns upright.

questions.stem: A pulse on a light rope reaches a join with a much heavier rope, where waves travel more slowly. What happens at the join?
options: Part reflects upright and part is transmitted inverted, moving more quickly
All of it reflects inverted, because the heavy rope acts like a fixed wall
All of it is transmitted upright, slowing down without any reflection
Part reflects inverted and part is transmitted upright, moving more slowly
questions.explanation: At a boundary between two media a wave is partly reflected and partly transmitted. The heavier rope behaves partly like a fixed end, so the reflected pulse is inverted. The transmitted pulse stays upright but moves more slowly in the heavier rope.

questions.stem: What is diffraction?
options: The combining of two waves to give a larger or smaller amplitude
The spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle
The bending of waves as they cross a boundary into a different medium
The bouncing of waves back from a hard surface at an equal angle
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading out of waves past the edges of a gap or obstacle. Bending at a boundary between media is refraction, bouncing back is reflection, and combining is superposition.

questions.stem: You can hear a person talking in a corridor through an open doorway, but cannot see them. Why?
options: Sound reflects from walls, but light is absorbed by every surface it strikes
Sound wavelengths are similar to the doorway's width, so sound diffracts widely
Sound travels much faster than light, so it reaches you around the corner first
Light wavelengths are similar to the doorway's width, so light cannot get through
questions.explanation: Diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is similar to the size of the gap. Speech has wavelengths from centimetres to metres, comparable to a doorway, so it spreads around the corner. Light has wavelengths below a micrometre, so it barely diffracts there.

questions.stem: What does the principle of superposition state?
options: Where waves overlap, they reflect off each other and swap their directions
Where waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the average of their displacements
Where waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of their displacements
Where waves overlap, the larger wave cancels the smaller one and continues alone
questions.explanation: When waves meet, the displacement at each point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. After they pass, each wave carries on unchanged, so they do not cancel or bounce off each other.

questions.stem: A pulse of amplitude +3.0 cm meets a pulse of amplitude −2.0 cm travelling the other way on a string. What is the displacement at the instant they fully overlap?
questions.explanation: By superposition the displacements add with their signs: +3.0 + (−2.0) = +1.0 cm. This is partly destructive interference. Adding the sizes gives +5.0 cm, which ignores that one pulse is inverted.

questions.stem: Two waves of the same frequency, with amplitudes 4.0 cm and 3.0 cm, overlap. What are the largest and smallest possible resultant amplitudes?
options: 12 cm and 1.0 cm
3.5 cm and 0.5 cm
7.0 cm and 1.0 cm
7.0 cm and 0 cm
questions.explanation: In phase, the waves interfere constructively: 4.0 + 3.0 = 7.0 cm. Exactly out of phase, they interfere destructively: 4.0 − 3.0 = 1.0 cm. Complete cancellation to zero needs equal amplitudes.

questions.stem: Two loudspeakers emit the same 346 Hz note in phase. A listener stands 4.0 m from one speaker and 5.5 m from the other. What does she hear? Use v = 346 m s⁻¹.
options: A quiet spot, because the path difference is one and a half wavelengths
A loud spot, because the path difference is one and a half wavelengths
A loud spot, because the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths
A quiet spot, because the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths
questions.explanation: The wavelength is 346/346 = 1.0 m, and the path difference is 5.5 − 4.0 = 1.5 m, which is 1.5 wavelengths. The waves arrive half a cycle out of phase and interfere destructively, giving a quiet spot. Whole-number path differences give loud spots.

questions.stem: How does a standing wave form?
options: Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose
Two waves of different frequencies travel in the same direction
A single wave slows down and stops when it reaches a boundary
A wave travels through a medium that is itself standing still
questions.explanation: A standing wave is the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude moving in opposite directions, usually an incident wave and its reflection. Constructive interference gives antinodes and destructive interference gives nodes.

questions.stem: In a standing wave, what is a node?
options: A point midway between two neighbouring antinodes on the same wave
A point that stays at zero displacement, from destructive interference
A point of maximum displacement, from constructive interference
A point where the two travelling waves are reflected from a boundary
questions.explanation: At a node the two travelling waves always cancel, so the medium there does not move. At an antinode they reinforce, giving the largest vibration. Nodes are midway between antinodes, but that position alone is not what defines them.

questions.stem: A standing wave on a string has nodes 0.25 m apart when the frequency is 400 Hz. What is the speed of waves on the string?
options: 100 m s⁻¹
400 m s⁻¹
200 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 m. Then v = fλ = 400 × 0.50 = 200 m s⁻¹. Treating the node spacing as a full wavelength gives 100 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A string 1.2 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in a standing wave with four loops. Which harmonic is this, and what is the wavelength?
options: Fourth harmonic, 0.60 m
Fourth harmonic, 0.30 m
Third harmonic, 0.80 m
Second harmonic, 1.2 m
questions.explanation: Each loop is half a wavelength, so four loops is the fourth harmonic, with L = 4λ/2. Then λ = 2L/4 = 2 × 1.2/4 = 0.60 m. Taking each loop as a full wavelength gives 0.30 m.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental of a vibrating string or air column?
options: Its lowest natural frequency, also called the first harmonic
Its highest natural frequency, at which it vibrates loudest
The frequency of the note that a tuning fork gives it at first
The difference between the frequencies of two of its harmonics
questions.explanation: The fundamental, or first harmonic, is the lowest frequency at which the system forms a standing wave. Higher harmonics are at higher frequencies. For a string or open pipe, the spacing between neighbouring harmonics equals the fundamental, but that is a result, not the definition.

questions.stem: What is the natural frequency of an object?
options: The frequency of the force that is used to make the object vibrate
The frequency at which the object absorbs the least energy possible
The frequency of sound that the object reflects most strongly
The frequency at which it vibrates when disturbed and then left alone
questions.explanation: Every object has natural frequencies, set by its size, shape and material, at which it vibrates freely after being struck or plucked. A driving force can have any frequency, and when it matches a natural frequency resonance occurs.

questions.stem: A string 0.90 m long, fixed at both ends, carries waves at 360 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of its third harmonic?
options: 600 Hz
200 Hz
400 Hz
questions.explanation: For a string, L = nλ/2, so for n = 3, λ = 2L/3 = 0.60 m. Then f = v/λ = 360/0.60 = 600 Hz. The fundamental is 200 Hz and the second harmonic is 400 Hz.

questions.stem: A pipe open at both ends is 0.50 m long. What is its fundamental frequency? Use v = 346 m s⁻¹.
options: 173 Hz
692 Hz
346 Hz
questions.explanation: For an open pipe, L = nλ/2, so the fundamental has λ = 2L = 1.0 m and f = 346/1.0 = 346 Hz. Using the closed-pipe result λ = 4L gives 173 Hz, and taking λ = L gives 692 Hz.

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end is 0.346 m long. What is the frequency of its next resonance above the fundamental? Use v = 346 m s⁻¹.
options: 500 Hz
250 Hz
750 Hz
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe, L = (2n − 1)λ/4. The fundamental (n = 1) has λ = 4L = 1.384 m, so f = 250 Hz. A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so the next resonance is three times the fundamental, 750 Hz. Giving 500 Hz assumes even harmonics exist, as in an open pipe.

questions.stem: A pipe open at both ends has a fundamental frequency of 220 Hz. What are its next two resonant frequencies?
options: 440 Hz and 660 Hz
660 Hz and 1100 Hz
330 Hz and 440 Hz
440 Hz and 880 Hz
questions.explanation: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends and produces every harmonic, so the frequencies are f, 2f, 3f and so on: 440 Hz and 660 Hz. Only odd multiples, 660 Hz and 1100 Hz, would be the pattern for a pipe closed at one end.

questions.stem: A 512 Hz tuning fork is held over a tube closed at the bottom. The first loud resonance occurs when the air column is 0.169 m long. What speed of sound does this give?
options: 692 m s⁻¹
346 m s⁻¹
173 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The first resonance in a closed tube is the fundamental, with L = λ/4, so λ = 4 × 0.169 = 0.676 m. Then v = fλ = 512 × 0.676 ≈ 346 m s⁻¹. Using λ = 2L, the open-pipe result, gives 173 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A guitarist halves the vibrating length of a string without changing its tension. What happens to its fundamental frequency?
options: It stays the same
It increases four times
It doubles
It halves
questions.explanation: The wave speed on the string depends on its tension and mass, which are unchanged. The fundamental wavelength is 2L, so halving L halves λ, and f = v/λ doubles.

questions.stem: A child on a swing is given a small push at the same point in each swing, and the swings grow higher. What is this an example of?
options: Resonance, because the pushes match the swing's natural frequency
Diffraction, because the swing spreads out around its pivot point
Refraction, because the swing changes speed as it changes height
Interference, because each push cancels part of the previous one
questions.explanation: When a periodic driving force matches a system's natural frequency, each push adds energy in step with the motion and the amplitude builds up. This is resonance.

questions.stem: Why does the amplitude of a system driven at its natural frequency become so large?
options: Energy is transferred to it efficiently, because each push is in step with its motion
The driving force becomes stronger as the system vibrates more and more quickly
The system stops losing any energy to its surroundings once resonance begins
The natural frequency of the system rises to match the driving force exactly
questions.explanation: At resonance, the driver always pushes in the direction the system is already moving, so energy is transferred efficiently each cycle. The amplitude grows until energy losses, such as friction, balance the input. Losses do not stop at resonance.

questions.stem: Tsunami warning systems use seismometers to detect large undersea earthquakes. Why can a warning be given before the tsunami reaches the coast?
options: Seismic waves can be heard in the air long before any water starts to move
Tsunamis do not form until several hours after the earthquake has ended
Seismic waves travel through rock much faster than a tsunami crosses the ocean
Tsunamis travel only along the sea floor, which slows them almost to a stop
questions.explanation: Seismic waves travel through Earth at several kilometres per second, far faster than a tsunami moves across the ocean. Detecting the earthquake and estimating its size gives time to warn coasts before the water waves arrive.

questions.stem: An acoustic engineer lines the back wall of a lecture theatre with soft, porous panels. What is the main purpose?
options: To raise the frequency of the speaker's voice for clarity
To absorb sound and reduce reflections that cause echoes
To reflect sound back towards the audience more strongly
To raise the speed of sound in the air of the theatre
questions.explanation: Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound strongly, causing echoes and reverberation. Soft, porous materials absorb much of the sound energy, reducing reflections. The panels do not change the speed or frequency of the sound.
